transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well… I’m here because occupational health basically told me I had to come in. They’re saying I’m not eating enough, and I suppose, technically, they’re not wrong, but I don’t see it quite the way they do.

Most days I’m fine with black coffee through the day, and then maybe I’ll have a plain yogurt, or later on a few bites of chicken if I feel I should. I don’t really sit down to a full meal. A full meal feels… I don’t know, excessive, like I’m letting my standards slip or giving in to something I should be able to control. That probably sounds odd, but in my line of work you get used to discipline meaning something, and I’ve always held myself to that. So they’ve made it into a concern, and that’s what brings me in.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently, or do you consider your weight to be below what would be expected for your height and build?

I mean… yes, I suppose I have, if you’re going by the usual measures. My uniform doesn’t fit the way it used to. It sort of hangs off me now, especially around the waist and shoulders, and I’ve had to keep tightening my belt past the old notches. At first I told myself that was just better discipline, you know, trimming down, keeping myself in order.

But the nurse at work was quite firm about it. She said my weight was dangerously low, which… I don’t know, that word bothered me more than the number did. “Dangerous” sounds dramatic. Even when she said it, part of me was still thinking, well, I could stand to be a bit sharper, a bit leaner. Not heavier. So yes, I know it’s below what they expect, but it doesn’t feel to me the way everyone else seems to think it should.
Do you find yourself actively avoiding eating certain foods, or going out of your way to prevent gaining weight, even if it means feeling hungry or uncomfortable?

Yes… I do. I don’t particularly like admitting it that plainly, but yes.

It’s not even always about a particular food, exactly, though there are definitely things I’ll steer clear of if I think they’ll sit heavy or make the number go the wrong way. It’s more that I’m always calculating what might make my weight go up, and if I think I’ve slipped, I’ll correct for it. If the scale is up even half a pound, I get this sort of jolt — like I’ve lost control of myself somehow. And then the whole day changes. I’ll cut back harder, have less than I planned, put off eating, tell myself I don’t need it yet.

I know half a pound probably sounds ridiculous to react to. I can hear that. But in the moment it doesn’t feel small. It feels like the start of putting weight back on, and I can’t stand that idea. I’d rather be hungry or uncomfortable than have that feeling that I’ve let it creep back.
Would you say that your weight or shape has a strong influence on how you see yourself or how you feel about your worth?

Yes… I think it does, more than I like to admit.

It’s not just a number, although the number matters. It’s when I look at myself — in the mirror, or even catching my reflection in a window at work — I don’t see what other people seem to be talking about. They say I look too thin, or they look concerned, but that’s not what jumps out at me. I look straight at my stomach, my waist, that area around my belt, and I’m checking whether I look controlled enough. Lean enough. If there’s any softness there, or if I think there is, it can ruin the whole day.

And I know that probably sounds vain, but it doesn’t feel like vanity. It feels like… if I look sharp and lean, then I can respect myself. Like I’ve kept myself in line. If I don’t, if I look heavier to myself, then I feel weak, sloppy, like I’ve failed at something basic. So yes, my weight and shape do affect how I see myself. Quite a lot, actually.
When you look at yourself, do you see your body differently than what others or objective measures suggest, such as perceiving yourself as heavier even when you are underweight?

Yes. I think that’s exactly the problem, though it’s hard to say because when I’m looking, it feels real.

When I look in the mirror, I don’t see what everyone else says they see. I don’t see “too thin” or whatever word they’re using. My eyes go straight to my stomach and my waist, almost automatically, like I’m inspecting whether I’ve let myself slip. I’ll stand there and turn a bit, check the line of my belt, the way my shirt sits, whether there’s any softness there. And if I think I look wider, or less lean, that becomes the thing I believe for the rest of the day.

I know objectively people are telling me something different. I know there are measures and numbers and uniforms hanging loose and all of that. But in the moment, none of that carries as much weight as what I think I see in the mirror. If I don’t look lean enough to myself, I feel like I’ve failed somehow. Like I can’t respect myself until I’ve got it under control again. So yes, I suppose I do see myself differently than other people do. It just doesn’t feel distorted when I’m in it. It feels like I’m seeing the part they’re missing.
Do you have a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even though you are already underweight?

Yes. I mean… yes, that’s probably the simplest answer.

Even if part of me understands what you’re saying — that I’m not at a weight where that should be the concern — it still feels like gaining weight would be this immediate, personal failure. If the scale is up even half a pound, I don’t just think, “Oh, that could be water or normal fluctuation.” I get this jolt, like something has gone wrong and I’ve lost control of myself.

And then I can’t leave it alone. I’ll spend the rest of the day trying to fix it — cutting back harder, delaying eating, making things smaller than I’d planned — because the idea of putting weight back on feels unbearable. It’s not some distant fear, either. It feels urgent, like if I don’t correct it right away it’ll keep going. So yes, I’m afraid of gaining weight. Very much.
